title: Electrical Safety in Construction (29 CFR 1926 Subpart K)
learningObjectives: Identify the four main electrical hazards on construction sites
Explain GFCI protection requirements for construction
Describe lockout/tagout requirements for construction electrical work
Recognise safe work distances from overhead power lines

content.text: Electricity is involved in roughly 8–10% of all construction fatalities. The four main electrical hazards are electrocution (death from electric shock), electric shock (injury), arc flash/blast (radiant heat, molten metal, pressure wave), and fires caused by electrical faults.

content.text: A device that monitors current flow through a circuit. If even a small imbalance (5 milliamps) is detected — indicating current is flowing somewhere it shouldn't (through a person to ground) — the GFCI trips in 1/40th of a second, before the shock becomes lethal.

OSHA 1926.404(b)(1) requires GFCI protection for all 120-volt, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles used by personnel at construction sites. This applies to temporary power (spider boxes, extension cords, power tools). GFCI protection OR an Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Program (AEGCP) is required.

The AEGCP is an alternative to GFCI. It requires a written program, colour-coded inspection of all cord sets and equipment before first use each day, and a three-prong testing procedure. In practice, GFCI is simpler and more commonly used.

items: Extension cords must be listed/approved (UL), rated for outdoor use where exposed to weather
Never remove the ground prong from a three-pronged plug
Extension cords are for temporary use only — not permanent wiring
No daisy-chaining (connecting multiple extension cords together to reach farther)
Inspect cords daily; remove from service if insulation is damaged, connectors cracked, or grounding prong missing
Keep cords out of doorways, windows, and areas where they can be damaged by vehicles or tools
Overhead cords must be at least 10 ft above pedestrian areas, 14 ft above vehicle areas

content.text: Contact with overhead power lines is the most common cause of electrocution on construction sites. OSHA 1926.1408 sets minimum approach distances based on line voltage. Always assume overhead lines are energised.

Before operating any equipment (cranes, excavators, aerial lifts, dump trucks) near overhead power lines, determine the voltage and establish the minimum approach distance. If you cannot maintain the distance, contact the utility to de-energise and ground the lines, or install insulating sleeves (only by the utility company).

When construction workers must work on electrical panels, switchgear, motors, or machinery, OSHA 1926.417 requires de-energising before work begins and using lockout/tagout procedures to prevent re-energisation. Only qualified persons may work on or near live parts.
A person who has received training in and demonstrated proficiency in the construction and operation of electrical equipment and installations, and the hazards involved. (1926.32(m))

A construction crew needs to install conduit inside an existing building with live panelboards. The electrical foreman identifies the circuit breakers, shuts them off, applies a personal lock, tests with a non-contact voltage tester, and posts a 'Do Not Re-energise' tag. Only after confirming no voltage does the crew begin conduit installation adjacent to the panel.

items: All 240-volt receptacles in temporary power distribution require GFCI or AEGCP
Metal frames and enclosures of electrical equipment must be grounded
Junction boxes must be covered; open knock-outs must be closed
Flexible cords must be continuous — no splicing or taping to repair insulation
Wet or damp locations require weatherproof boxes and listed wet-location equipment

content.text: Gulf Context: Electrical fatalities are a top concern on Gulf megaprojects. Aramco SEMP Life-Saving Rule requires an approved isolation certificate (equivalent to OSHA LOTO) before any electrical work. In the UAE, Abu Dhabi's OSHAD-SF requires all electrical tasks on energised systems above 50V AC to have an energised electrical work permit. ADNOC projects require IEC 60900-rated insulated tools. In Qatar, hot work and electrical isolation are managed under QatarEnergy's Permit to Work system — which includes a separate Electrical Isolation Certificate.
